newsitem.title: INDIA: New vote for Mother Teresa successor to be set.
newsitem.headline: New vote for Mother Teresa successor to be set.

text.p: The Missionaries of Charity postponed this weekend's vote to choose a successor to Mother Teresa for technical reasons, sources close to the Roman Catholic order said on Wednesday.
They said a new date for the election would be set shortly.

"This time there are 123 members in the General Chapter or the electoral college and they have come from all over the world. It is only natural that the members of the electoral college will need more time to get to know each other," the sources told Reuters.
The electoral college is comprised of representatives from various sections of the order, which has about 4,500 nuns.

"The concerned Sisters cannot have frank discussions without knowing each other properly. And frank discussions are absolutely necessary during the deliberations," said the sources who did not wish to be identified.

The senior nuns began a two-week retreat on January 16 to select a successor to the 1979 Nobel Peace Prize winner, who has been taken to hospital three times since August, twice for heart trouble and once after hitting her head in a fall.
Set to end on January 31, the retreat was to be followed by several meetings of the General Chapter before the election by secret ballot next Sunday.

A statement from the office of Archbishop of Calcutta Henry D'Souza on Tuesday gave no explanation for the postponement and did not set a new date for the election. It said the ailing 86-year-old nun had agreed to the postponement.
The elections for the Superior General, the Assistant General and three council members will be held only at the end of the deliberations, said the sources.
The sources said "seminars", which are extensions of the retreat, are the only time when the members of the electoral college can get to know one another.

"All the 123 Sisters are now participating in the seminars and the time-frame for the seminars has been extended so that the participants could know each other better and have frank discussions during deliberations," they said.

The 1979 Nobel Peace Prize winner, known affectionately as "Mother", had wanted to step down in 1990, one year after she was fitted with a heart pacemaker, because of ill health. But her colleagues asked her to stay on.
Mother Teresa has led the order since the start, shaping the mission's work in 111 countries with her strong, charismatic personality.
But she has decided to retire as the order's superior general because of heart, kidney and lung problems.
A regular six-year election by secret ballot set for last September had to be delayed because Mother Teresa was sent to hospital in August with heart problems, pneumonia and malaria.
